genZNote: Lives peacefully in everyone's gumline until dental trauma gives it a way in — then it forms the infamous 'sulfur granules.'

morphology.arrangement: Branching filaments, sometimes fragmenting into rods

habitat.naturalHabitat: Human oral cavity, particularly gingival crevices and tonsillar crypts
habitat.hostAssociation: Normal commensal of the human mouth, GI tract, and female genital tract in small numbers
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Not free-living in the environment; strictly host-associated

culture.growthCharacteristics: Slow-growing strict anaerobe; may take a week or more
culture.colonyMorphology: Classic 'molar tooth' colonies on prolonged anaerobic culture

identificationClues: Yellow 'sulfur granules' in draining pus or tissue are a classic bedside clue (not actually sulfur — clumps of filamentous organism)
Gram-positive branching filaments, catalase-negative, distinguishing it from Nocardia (which is often catalase-positive and partially acid-fast)
Requires strict anaerobic conditions and prolonged incubation to culture
Disease typically follows dental work, trauma, or mucosal disruption that lets the normal oral commensal invade tissue

virulenceFactors: Forms dense filamentous colonies (granules) that resist phagocytosis and antibiotic penetration
clinicalImportance.transmission: Endogenous — arises from the patient's own oral/GI flora after mucosal breach, not transmitted person-to-person
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: Classically follows dental extraction, jaw trauma, or long-term intrauterine device use
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Not acid-fast, which helps distinguish actinomycosis from mycobacterial or nocardial disease on smear

examFacts.importantTest: Sulfur granules on gross exam; anaerobic culture with 'molar tooth' colonies
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Normal oral commensal that causes disease only after mucosal disruption — an endogenous, not exogenous, infection
